The Forty Percent That Isn't There: A Deep Treatment of the Sean Ellis PMF Survey

Two product leaders, two surveys, two numbers straddling the famous line — and a sampling problem large enough to swallow both.

1. Two decisions, three weeks apart

On 19 March 2026, Nandita Varma, VP of Product at Aakarna Labs, sat in a Gurugram conference room with a pricing memo she did not believe. Aakarna sells an AI-native sales-call intelligence product: it listens to inside-sales calls, scores them against a rubric the customer configures, and writes the CRM notes the rep would otherwise skip. Thirty-eight accounts, 412 paid seats, ₹3.1 crore of annual recurring revenue, most of it still on design-partner pricing signed in 2024 at a third of list. The memo proposed moving nineteen accounts to list at renewal — ₹5.4 crore of ARR if nobody left, ₹3.8 crore if the four largest walked.

Her board had been unambiguous: do not reprice before you know whether the product has pull. So in February she ran the Sean Ellis survey against her weekly-active seat holders. Of 380 invited, 164 answered, and 61 — 37.2 percent — said they would be very disappointed if Aakarna disappeared. The number sat just under the benchmark everyone in the room had heard of, and the debate that followed was not about the product. It was about whether 37.2 differed meaningfully from 40.

Three weeks later and 1,400 kilometres south-west, Aniruddh Kale faced a mirror-image problem in Pune. Kale is Head of Product at Shravandhara Instruments, which makes a ₹34,000 behind-the-ear hearing aid for the Indian mid-market, bundled with a companion app. The app is where the software business lives: ₹299 a month for adaptive noise profiles, remote audiologist tuning and a hearing-health log. On 6 April 2026 he had to recommend either folding those features into the device price and shutting the subscription down, or funding a second app team at roughly ₹1.9 crore a year.

His survey looked like good news. Of 600 app-active owners invited, 274 responded and 121 — 44.2 percent — chose "very disappointed." Above the line. Yet the subscription churned at 6.1 percent a month, annualising to half the paying base. His finance counterpart in Singapore, Wei-Ling Tan, put it bluntly on a 7 a.m. call: "Either your survey is wrong or your billing system is. Both cannot be describing the same customers."

Both were. Understanding why requires taking the instrument apart.

2. The idea, its history, and the four positions people actually hold

The survey is one item: How would you feel if you could no longer use [product]? with three options — very disappointed, somewhat disappointed, not disappointed (it isn't really that useful to me). The reported score is the share choosing "very disappointed" among respondents drawn from users who have genuinely used the product. Sean Ellis, a growth marketer whose early work included Dropbox, LogMeIn, Eventbrite and Xobni, developed it around 2008–2010 and packaged it as a free tool, survey.io. He was not defining product-market fit philosophically but solving an operating problem: he kept being hired to scale acquisition for companies whose products could not hold the users that acquisition would buy, and he needed a cheap pre-flight check. Across roughly a hundred companies he advised, those clearing about 40 percent found growth comparatively easy and those below it did not.

Two things about that origin are usually forgotten. The benchmark is an empirical regularity from one advisor's non-random sample of mostly early-2000s Western software companies, not a derived constant. And Ellis's framing was asymmetric: below 40 percent, do not scale spend; above it, spend is likelier to compound. He never claimed the number measured product quality or that it was comparable across categories.

Four positions have since hardened, and an expert can state each in the form its strongest advocate would sign.

The growth-gate position (Ellis and most growth practitioners). Signs: "the score is a spend gate; a product below roughly 40 percent among genuinely active users should not have paid acquisition poured on it." Will not sign: "40 percent is a constant across categories."

The revealed-preference position (retention-cohort analysts). Signs: "behaviour dominates stated preference; a flattening retention curve is direct evidence and a survey is at best a noisy proxy for it." Will not sign: "a survey number may override a declining cohort curve."

The measurement position (survey methodologists). Signs: "the follow-ups are the real value; the headline is a single-item, three-point, unanchored scale on a self-selected frame, and non-response bias almost always exceeds sampling error." Will not sign: "a PMF percentage means anything without a stated frame and response rate."

The segmentation position (Rahul Vohra's Superhuman formulation, published in 2018 and now the most-copied extension). Signs: "the score is a steering wheel, not a verdict: discard the 'not disappointed', find the high-expectation customer inside the 'very disappointed', and build the roadmap from the 'somewhat disappointed' who already name your core benefit." Will not sign: "the blended number is the output."

These four do not reconcile, and pretending otherwise is the commonest move in PM teaching. The first two disagree about whether a survey should ever change a spending decision; the last two about whether the percentage should be reported at all.

3. Mechanics in depth, including the arithmetic nobody runs

Expert practice differs from textbook practice in four places: the frame, the uncertainty around the estimate, the non-response bound, and the decomposition of the blend into segment mix. The first is widely taught; the other three are where the work lives.

3.1 The frame is a modelling choice, not an administrative detail

Nandita defined "active" as a seat holder whose calls were processed in at least three of the preceding four weeks, excluding 27 percent of paid seats. Every exclusion is a hypothesis: that people below the threshold have no informed view on losing the product. It is false in an important way — a rep who abandoned Aakarna in week two over poor Hindi-English code-mixed transcription holds a very informed view, and is removed from numerator and denominator alike. The frame does not trim noise; it encodes an assumption about who counts.

3.2 Sampling error: the interval, not the point

A proportion estimated from a sample carries a standard error of √(p̂(1−p̂)/n). For Aakarna, p̂ = 0.372 and n = 164: √(0.372 × 0.628 / 164) = 0.0377, or 3.8 points, giving a 95 percent interval of 29.8 to 44.6 percent. For Shravandhara, p̂ = 0.442 and n = 274 gives 0.0300 and an interval of 38.3 to 50.1 percent. Both contain 40. Nandita's "just below the line" and Kale's "just above" are statistically the same statement: we cannot tell. Resolving a proportion near 0.4 to within ±5 points at 95 percent confidence requires n ≈ 1.96² × 0.25 / 0.05² = 384 completed responses; to within ±3 points, n ≈ 1,067. Neither company was close, and neither had noticed.

3.3 The non-response bound, which dwarfs everything else

Aakarna's response rate was 164 / 380 = 43.2 percent — unusually good. Still, 216 invitees said nothing. If every one would have chosen "not disappointed," the true share among invitees is 61 / 380 = 16.1 percent; if every one "very disappointed," 277 / 380 = 72.9 percent. The manifest bound is [16.1, 72.9], a span of 57 points against a sampling interval of 15. The usual assumption — that non-respondents resemble respondents — is precisely what the instrument's known pathology contradicts, since indifferent users are likeliest to ignore a survey about a product they do not care about. The implication is not paralysis but three habits: treat the score as optimistic, report response rate beside it, and read a score rising while response rate falls as an artefact.

3.4 Decomposition: the blend is a weighted average, so mix moves it

Any blended score is Σ wᵢ pᵢ, where wᵢ is a segment's share of respondents and pᵢ its within-segment score. Aakarna's 164 respondents split into 118 sales reps and 46 managers and ops leads — the people who configure the rubric and read the dashboards.

Two consequences follow. The first is diagnostic: the people who pay for Aakarna love it and the people who use it are lukewarm — the classic signature of a compliance product, bought to ease a manager's reporting and tolerated by the person it observes. The second is arithmetic and more dangerous. If the next four accounts are flatter organisations with more managers per rep, shifting the mix to 60/40, the blend becomes 0.60 × 0.314 + 0.40 × 0.522 = 39.7 percent — a 2.5-point gain produced entirely by who answered. A blended score on a quarterly dashboard tracks customer mix as much as product.

Kale's decomposition told a different story with the same machinery. Splitting his 274 respondents by daily use of the adaptive-profile feature gave 96 daily tuners at 64.6 percent and 178 occasional users at 33.1 percent. The blend, 121/274 = 44.2 percent, describes nobody. There is a real, intense product inside Shravandhara's app, used by a third of app-active owners, and a wrapper the rest tolerate because it came with the device.

4. When the instrument applies, stated as testable claims

The survey earns its keep only when four conditions hold. Each is falsifiable, and each can be checked against the two protagonists.

Claim 1: the counterfactual must be imaginable. The question asks the respondent to simulate a world without the product, which works only when a substitute exists and switching is conceivable. Aakarna: holds weakly — 44 of 164 named a general AI assistant and manual CRM entry as their alternative, and cheap counterfactuals depress scores for reasons unrelated to how well the product works. Shravandhara: partially fails, since losing the app does not mean losing the hearing aid, which keeps working on its default profile; respondents answered about a feature bundle while imagining the loss of their hearing.

Claim 2: usage must have become a habit. Disappointment-at-loss proxies switching cost plus routine. Aakarna: holds; three-of-four-weeks usage is a genuine routine. Shravandhara: holds for the daily tuners and fails for the occasional users — exactly the split the decomposition found.

Claim 3: one product, one relationship. The "it" must name a single thing the respondent can picture. Aakarna: holds. Shravandhara: fails — "it" spans ₹34,000 of hardware already paid for and a ₹299 subscription cancellable tonight.

Claim 4: behavioural data must be too thin or too slow to answer directly. The most-ignored condition. Aakarna: holds; with 38 accounts and eighteen months of history, retention cohorts are too small to read. Shravandhara: fails outright — Kale had 6.1 percent monthly churn, a direct measurement of precisely what the survey was proxying. When behaviour and stated preference conflict, behaviour wins and the survey's job shrinks to explaining why.

A fifth situation makes the instrument misleading rather than merely uninformative: when the product is mandatory. A GST e-invoicing module, a regulator-mandated audit trail, a corporate expense tool with no alternative — all score high, because "I could no longer use it" implies a compliance failure rather than an inconvenience. High disappointment there measures the penalty for non-use, not pull.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

Multi-product companies face a referent problem. When Nisunaa Learning, a Hyderabad K-12 company, surveys users of its test-prep app, its doubt-solving chat and its school gradebook under one brand, "it" resolves differently for every respondent and the blend averages three products weighted by whoever opened email. Mature firms survey per surface and per job, never per brand — though they report per brand to the board, because that is the number that fits on a slide.

Two-sided markets require two surveys and forbid one number. At Pratishruti Exchange, a Nashik wholesale spice marketplace, a seller's disappointment turns on income substitution — could they sell the same lot to the same buyer by phone tomorrow? — while a buyer's turns on assortment and credit terms. Averaging them produces a figure with no referent.

Hardware-plus-software is Shravandhara's case: sunk physical cost contaminates the counterfactual upward, the prospect of a degraded-but-working device downward. Expert practice scopes the question explicitly — "if the subscription features were withdrawn but your device kept working as it does today" — which is no longer Ellis's instrument but a far more honest one.

AI-native products strain it differently. Aakarna's value is partly model accuracy, which drifts: a January vendor upgrade raised code-mixed transcription accuracy from 81 to 89 percent, so the thing evaluated is not stable between rounds, and the substitute set is fluid too. A falling score can mean the product got worse or that substitutes got better, and the survey cannot distinguish them — which is exactly what a pricing decision turns on.

At the organisational seam, the recurring failure is ownership. When the score sits in a growth team's OKR, the frame migrates — quietly, defensibly, one reasonable tweak at a time — toward users likely to answer well. Firms that handle this well separate measurement from target: research owns the frame and the fielding, product owns the response, and the number is reported with frame, response rate and segment cuts attached. Most say they do this; few do, and the tell is whether anyone can produce last quarter's invite-list definition without asking three people.

6. Nine distinctions between an expert and a competent practitioner

One: the expert reads the interval before the point estimate. The competent practitioner reports 37.2 percent; the expert reports 37 ± 4 and asks what decision would change if the truth were 44. Tell-tale sign: a score shown to one decimal with no n beside it. The obvious reading — that precision signals rigour — is backwards; the decimal usually means nobody computed a standard error.

Two: the expert treats the score as a mix statistic. Because the blend is Σ wᵢpᵢ, a moving score has two possible causes and the naive reading assumes one. Tell-tale sign: a score that improves in a quarter with nothing consequential shipped, or worsens in a quarter of good releases. The first move is to hold weights at the prior mix and recompute; if the shift disappears, the customer base changed, not the product.

Three: the expert knows the score is bounded above by the frame's selectivity. Restricting to three-of-four-week actives all but guarantees a respectable number, because the frame has already removed everyone the product failed. Tell-tale sign: a strong score beside a weak activation rate. The obvious reading is "we have fit, we need better onboarding"; the sharper one is that the survey describes survivors and is silent on the ninety percent who never reached the frame.

Four: the expert reads the free-text before the percentage. The "what would you use instead" answers define the competitive set empirically, and they frequently name something the strategy deck does not contain. Tell-tale sign: a team that quotes its score but cannot name its three commonest substitutes. Aakarna believed it competed with two conversation-intelligence vendors; its users named a general AI assistant, a shared spreadsheet, and "nothing, I'd just stop writing notes."

Five: the expert distrusts improvement more than decline. Scores drift upward for at least four reasons unrelated to the product: survivor accumulation as weak users churn out of the frame, mix shift toward heavier segments, falling response rates concentrating enthusiasts, and send-timing that follows a support success. Tell-tale sign: a score up three points on a response rate down eight. The obvious reading is momentum; the correct one is a friendlier denominator.

Six: the expert uses the "somewhat disappointed" group as the roadmap. This is the Vohra move and it is genuinely non-obvious. Those in the middle who name your core benefit as their primary value are the population a product change can convert; those naming a peripheral benefit are not worth building for. Tell-tale sign: a team reporting only the very-disappointed share and discarding the rest of the file. The middle group is where the instrument turns prescriptive rather than merely evaluative.

Seven: the expert checks whether behavioural data already answers the question. A survey is a proxy, and where a direct measurement exists it dominates. Tell-tale sign: a survey commissioned by a company with eighteen months of cohort data and a stable definition of a retained user. The obvious reading — more evidence is better — ignores that the non-response bound is consistent with almost any retention curve, so the survey cannot contradict the logs and can only soften them.

Eight: the expert scopes the counterfactual in bundled products. Where the product is one layer of something the customer already owns, the unscoped question measures the bundle. Tell-tale sign: a high score beside high churn on the cancellable layer — Kale's situation exactly. The obvious reading is that the survey is wrong; the accurate one is that it answered a different question from the billing system, and both are right.

Nine: the expert holds the benchmark loosely and the trend tightly. Base rates differ by category: utilities with an acute, recurring job clear 40 percent readily, discretionary products often plateau in the twenties while thriving, and mandatory tools clear it meaninglessly. Tell-tale sign: a fundraising narrative in which crossing 40 is the headline. The expert compares the product to its own prior rounds on an unchanged frame, treating the absolute number as the least informative thing on the page.

7. How it differs by product type and by stage — and where it does not

In consumer products the instrument is closest to its design intent: one user, one relationship, large samples cheaply available, the hazards being frame selectivity and the discretionary-category base rate. In B2B and enterprise it fractures along the buyer–user seam, as Exhibit A shows; report user and buyer scores separately, because a compliance product's buyer score flatters the whole. Platforms and marketplaces need separate instruments and no blended figure, the sides facing structurally different substitution economics.

For hardware and physical goods the survey is weakest: the counterfactual is confounded by sunk cost, and purchase frequency is too low for "habit" to mean what the question assumes. For AI-native products the instrument is not structurally different — worth saying plainly, since the claim that AI breaks everything is usually overdone — but two parameters change: what is measured drifts between rounds as models update, and the substitute set is unusually elastic, so score movements carry less information about the product than in a stable category.

Stage does not change the mechanics; it changes the statistics. At seed, samples of 40 to 80 give intervals of ±10 to ±15 points, useful only for detecting extremes and useless near the line. At growth stage, samples permit segment-level reading, where the instrument is most valuable. At scale, the blended company number degenerates into a mix statistic, and the only defensible use is per-surface, per-segment, on a fixed frame, tracked as a trend.

8. Three worked examples, one of them a failure

8.1 Aakarna Labs: the segmented read changes the decision

Nandita's team had planned to reprice all nineteen design-partner accounts; the decomposition suggested a different cut. Of the 38 accounts, 14 had a manager-to-rep ratio above 1:6 and rubrics edited within 60 days — the behavioural signature of the segment scoring 52 percent. Re-running the score on respondents from those 14 gave 29 of 58, or 50.0 percent, interval roughly 37 to 63; among the rest, 32 of 106, or 30.2 percent. Aakarna repriced eleven accounts from the first group and held the others at partner pricing on a twelve-month commitment. Nine of eleven renewed at list, two negotiated down, and ARR reached ₹4.6 crore rather than the memo's ₹5.4 crore, with no logo churn.

8.2 Shravandhara Instruments: the score that meant the opposite of what it said

Kale re-fielded in May with a scoped question: "if the app's subscription features were withdrawn but your hearing aid continued working exactly as it does today, how would you feel?" The score fell from 44.2 to 21.7 percent (58 of 267) — 51.0 percent among daily tuners, 9.4 percent among occasional users. That reconciled the survey with the 6.1 percent churn and reframed the decision. Kale neither funded a second app team nor shut the subscription down: he moved adaptive profiles into a higher-priced device SKU, kept a ₹149 tier for the remote-audiologist feature the daily tuners named most, and cut subscription marketing to zero. Subscription revenue fell 38 percent, gross margin per device rose, and churn on the remaining tier fell to 2.4 percent.

8.3 Pratishruti Exchange: the approach failed, and why

Pratishruti's growth lead surveyed sellers who had transacted in the preceding 30 days, got 46 percent very disappointed on 210 responses, and read it as a green light for ₹6 crore of seller-acquisition spend across three commodity lanes. Twelve months later, month-six seller retention was 19 percent and the acquired cohort was worse than the organic one it replaced.

Three errors compounded. The frame — transacted in 30 days — mechanically selected the already-retained on a platform whose median seller transacts quarterly, so the survey measured attachment among survivors of a filter that itself encoded the outcome. The score was never decomposed by lane; re-run later it gave 61 percent in turmeric, where Pratishruti had buyer density, and 28 percent in chilli and coriander, where it did not. And the free-text was never read: the modal answer to "what would you use instead" was "call the same four buyers directly" — the platform's value was a directory the seller had already memorised, which decays to zero by design.

Recovery took three quarters. The team rebuilt the frame stratified by tenure rather than recency, re-fielded, and reported 24 percent — a 22-point fall caused entirely by a better frame. They withdrew from two lanes, concentrated on turmeric, and replaced the survey as primary instrument with a month-six repeat-transaction cohort, keeping the survey for its free-text. Month-six retention in that lane reached 41 percent within a year.

9. Failure modes, their early warnings and the cost of late detection

The failures below are ordered by cost of late detection, not frequency. Each has a diagnostic cheap enough to ask in a meeting.

The pattern is the same across all six: each failure is created when the frame is chosen and discovered when money is committed, and the interval between is where cost accumulates. Hence the disproportionate expert effort on the invite list and the comparatively little on the analysis, which is only arithmetic.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Is the 40 percent threshold portable? Defenders argue that a decade and a half of practitioner use has not dislodged it, that its asymmetric form — a floor below which not to scale spend — is robust to category variation in a way a two-sided target would not be, and that its value is coordinative: a shared, imperfect line lets investors and operators talk. Critics note that the original sample was one advisor's client base, selected on having sought growth help, that no published replication establishes base rates by category, and that scores cluster well below 40 in discretionary categories that nonetheless grow. For the defenders to be wrong, products below 40 percent would have to scale acquisition as profitably as those above once category and stage are controlled. That study does not exist, which is itself informative about how much weight the line can carry.

Should a survey ever override behaviour? The revealed-preference camp says never: stated preference under hypothetical loss is weak and its non-response bias unbounded, so conflicts resolve in favour of the logs. The growth-gate camp answers that behaviour is often unavailable at the moment of decision — pre-launch, at small n, in long-cycle enterprise products where retention takes eighteen months to read — and that a biased estimate available now beats an unbiased one available too late. For the behaviourists to be wrong, there must be decisions where the survey's information exceeds the cost of its bias; Aakarna, with 38 accounts, is plausibly one. For the growth-gate camp to be wrong, survey-informed decisions at small n would have to do no better than judgement without them.

Should the headline percentage be reported at all? The measurement and segmentation camps converge on scepticism from different directions — one because the estimate is fragile, the other because a scalar discards the structure that makes the instrument useful — while boards still want one comparable number. The disagreement is institutional rather than technical and remains unresolved: a firm that stops reporting a headline loses comparability with peers who still do, and comparability, even of a poor measure, has real coordinating value. Nobody here is making a mistake; they are weighing different costs.

Do AI-native products need a different instrument? Some argue that fluid substitution and drifting model quality make period-to-period comparison meaningless, and that task-completion measures should replace the survey. Others call this a difference of degree — substitutes and quality have always drifted — and abandoning a working instrument for a fashion a bad trade. There is not yet enough longitudinal evidence to adjudicate, and honest practitioners say so.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied the survey runs it, reports a percentage and compares it to 40. Someone who has internalised it starts from the decision: what is about to be committed — spend, headcount, a repricing — and what range of scores would change that commitment. If no plausible score changes it, they do not field at all. They write the frame down before seeing data and refuse to alter it between rounds, holding any exploratory frame separately. They report n, response rate, interval and at least two segment cuts, and lead with the cuts. They read the free-text first and the percentage last. They know their category's base rate or admit they do not. And when survey and logs disagree, they assume the logs are right and use the survey to explain the disagreement rather than dispute it. The signature of mastery is reluctance to field: an expert runs the instrument less often than a novice and gets more from each round.

12. What the two protagonists decided

Nandita Varma treated 37.2 percent as neither failing grade nor near-miss but as a mix statistic. She decomposed it, found the score carried by rubric owners rather than reps, and concluded that Aakarna was a manager's product with a rep's price tag. She repriced the eleven accounts whose behaviour matched the enthusiastic segment, held the rest, and redirected two engineers onto the code-mixed transcription problem the reps' free-text named most. Her board memo reported interval and response rate, and said explicitly that the company could not distinguish its score from 44 percent.

Aniruddh Kale did the harder thing: he assumed his own favourable number was wrong, re-fielded with a scoped counterfactual, watched the score fall 22 points and let it change the plan. Shravandhara's app is now a device feature with a narrow paid tier, and the ₹1.9 crore funds an audiologist-network expansion. The survey did not tell him what to do; it told him which of two contradictory sources to believe, and that was the whole of its value.

Discussion questions.

1. Aakarna's non-response bound is [16.1, 72.9] percent. On what grounds — if any — is Nandita entitled to act on a 37.2 percent point estimate at all, and what would you require her to show before approving the repricing?

2. Kale's survey and his billing system disagreed, and he resolved the conflict by changing the survey. When would you resolve such a conflict the other way, and how would you defend that to a board?

3. Pratishruti's honest score, 24 percent, came from a better frame rather than a worse product. If a competitor reports 46 percent on Pratishruti's original frame, what should an investor conclude — and what would make the comparison meaningful?

13. Going deeper

Survey design
Frame, wording and timing are where the score is actually determined; the vocabulary for defending or attacking any reported number.
Product-market fit
The construct the survey proxies, and why a scalar cannot carry a state that is segment-specific, time-varying and partly behavioural.
Sampling and representativeness
The non-response bound in §3.3 is the discipline in miniature; stratification and weighting narrow it rather than ignore it.
Descriptive statistics for PMs
Standard errors, intervals and weighted averages: the minimum arithmetic for reading a proportion honestly. Exhibit A is only a weighted mean read carefully.
Conjoint and MaxDiff
Quantifies trade-offs among attributes and prices — the natural next instrument once fit exists and you need to know what to charge for it.
Quantitative concept testing
The same stated-preference machinery before a product exists, where no behavioural data can contradict it — its biases both more dangerous and better studied.
NPS, CSAT and CES
The instruments PMF scores are most often confused with; knowing what each measures prevents treating high satisfaction as evidence of attachment.
Consumer panels and syndicated data
Supplies the category base rates the 40 percent debate lacks, so "is 31 percent good here?" can be answered with evidence rather than folklore.

Ishara Technologies Thirty-eight per cent, and the question of what it is thirty-eight per cent of

Discovery & Design → Quantitative & Market Research. For class discussion only. Ishara Technologies, Izdihaar Trading and Istaara Ventures are fictitious, as are all individuals named. Other firms, regulators and institutions are real and appear only as market context.

1. Diwali night, Pune

At a quarter past eleven on the night of Sunday, 8 November 2026, the crackers over Baner had thinned to the occasional late one, and Chaitrali Rautray was still at the dining table with her laptop and a plate of untouched karanji. In under twenty-two hours the board pack had to go to six people in four time zones, and the slide she could not write was slide four.

Slide four was supposed to say what the September product–market fit survey had found. For the second time, Ishara had asked its shopkeeper users how disappointed they would be if the product disappeared tomorrow. In March the answer had been 41.0 per cent very disappointed. On the Monday after the September fielding closed the growth dashboard put up 44.0 per cent and the Bengaluru engineering channel posted a rocket emoji. Eleven days later Celine Rouleau, in Toronto, rebuilt the query from the raw event table and sent four lines beginning, I think the dashboard is dividing by the wrong number.

It was. On the base Celine argued for, the figure was 38.0 per cent. Sean Ellis's much-quoted benchmark — written into the bridge-financing term sheet Chaitrali had open in another tab — was 40 per cent. The difference between 44 and 38 was a milestone met or a milestone missed, produced entirely by a choice of denominator nobody had been asked to ratify.

Since then it had got worse, not clearer. A panel study commissioned in September by Istaara Ventures' own research desk came back at 24.0 per cent. One segment of users scored 50.0 per cent and another 28.9; the higher-scoring one supplied about a quarter of revenue, the lower-scoring one three-quarters of the user base. Depending on the weighting she could defend 33.5, 38.0 or 39.1 per cent, and had spent Diwali afternoon establishing that all three were arithmetically correct.

What she had not worked out was what any of them meant about the product.

2. The company, and the decision of July 2024

Ishara was founded in Pune in October 2021 by Chandresh Radhakrishnan, nine years a field-sales man for a paints distributor, and Charuta Ranadive, who had built reconciliation systems for a Bengaluru payments firm. Ishara Udhaar launched in February 2022 as a Marathi- and Hindi-first credit ledger for neighbourhood retailers: the shopkeeper recorded what each customer owed, and Ishara reminded the customer. It grew by one shopkeeper showing another, and by October 2026 had 8,41,000 registered accounts, 1,46,000 of them active in a month.

The decision that constrains everything today was taken in July 2024, when Ishara closed a ₹46 crore Series A led by Istaara Ventures at a ₹310 crore post-money valuation. In the same fortnight Cormac Rafferty, hired out of New Jersey to open the Gulf channel, brought in Izdihaar Trading, a Dubai foodstuffs distributor. Izdihaar would standardise its 180 downstream outlets on Ishara — but only if Ishara built a distributor tier: multi-outlet rollups, credit limits, GST e-invoicing, and a VAT variant for the UAE.

Charuta put two options to the board: the distributor tier, two quarters of work for a committed customer, or a rewrite of the Udhaar ledger core, written in eleven weeks in 2021 and never revisited, which would cut the twelve-second median save time on a 2 GB Android phone. The first had a contract attached. The second had an engineering argument.

The board chose the contract. Signed on 11 July 2024 and running to 10 July 2027, it carries 180 seats at ₹1,499 a month — ₹2,69,820 a month, or ₹32.38 lakh a year — and a clause requiring Arabic invoicing and UAE VAT fields by 31 January 2027, with a service credit of ₹18 lakh if the date is missed. Twenty-eight months on, the ledger core is unrewritten, and 36,450 of Ishara's 48,600 core-active accounts use nothing else.

3. The industry

India's shopkeeper-software market is crowded at the free end and thin at the paying end. Khatabook and OkCredit established the digital-ledger category and then broadened towards payments and lending; Vyapar, Tally, Zoho Books and Marg hold the billing and accounting ground. None has found it easy to charge a single-outlet kirana ₹149 a month for bookkeeping alone. The money sits downstream of the ledger, which is why Ishara launched Ishara Collect in March 2025: Collect turns a ledger entry into a UPI collect request, so the customer settles from PhonePe or Google Pay instead of promising to come on Friday. Ishara holds no payment aggregator authorisation from the Reserve Bank of India and rides on a licensed partner. Collect is the only part of the product shopkeepers reliably pay for, because it visibly produces cash.

Three regulatory facts bear on the decision. GST e-invoicing now reaches businesses well below the old thresholds, which pulls the distributor tier's buyers towards compliant software and is why Izdihaar came to Ishara. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and its notified rules have changed what Ishara may do with the phone numbers in its users' ledgers: those numbers belong to the shopkeepers' customers, and the consent architecture for reaching them — survey invitations included — was rebuilt between June and September 2026 under Cheryl Raghunathan's programme in Singapore. And ONDC's retail onboarding has made some distributors curious about bypassing their own channel, making Izdihaar a nervous customer — and Ishara's whole exposure beyond India: 180 of its 1,220 paying distributor-tier accounts sit under it in Dubai and Sharjah, on the only contract in the company with a penalty clause.

4. The situation, in sequence

Wave 1 was fielded from 9 to 19 March 2026 by Chintan Rasal's growth team using a web-dashboard intercept. 31,200 accounts then met the core-experience screen; 6,000 were invited, 1,548 started, 1,200 answered the disappointment question, and 492 of those said very disappointed — 41.0 per cent. The team noted that Ishara had cleared the 40 per cent bar and moved on. Nobody noticed the intercept was web-only, and that single-outlet Udhaar users are overwhelmingly on Android.

Two things then changed. Collect grew, giving the web dashboard a population of daily reconcilers; and the DPDP consent rebuild gave Ishara its first lawful WhatsApp channel to its account holders. So when Chintan fielded wave 2 from 14 to 24 September he did the obviously better thing: a simple random sample of 9,000 from the 48,600 accounts meeting the screen, invited on the dashboard where the account had a web session and over WhatsApp where it did not. 2,310 started; 1,800 answered the disappointment question.

The dashboard reported 44.0 per cent. It was scoring only respondents who had finished all five questions — 1,364 people — of whom 600 had said very disappointed. Celine's objection: the top box is the most engaged answer, so very-disappointed users complete free-text follow-ups at a higher rate than the indifferent, and conditioning on completion selects for the thing being measured. On the base of everyone who answered the question at all, 684 of the 1,800 were very disappointed: 38.0 per cent (Exhibits 1 and 2).

Celine then did the thing that unsettled the company. Cross-tabulating by segment and by invitation channel (Exhibit 3), she showed the respondent pool was nothing like the user base: Collect users were 18.0 per cent of the eligible population and 35.6 per cent of respondents, because the web intercept reached them and because daily reconcilers answer surveys. Weighted back to the eligible population the same 684 answers give 33.5 per cent; weighted by revenue, 39.1 (Exhibit 4).

On 6 October the investor's research desk reported its panel study: 750 shopkeepers from a market-research panel, 180 very disappointed, 24.0 per cent. Chandresh said the panel was garbage. Celine, after an afternoon with the screening data, said it was not: 318 of the 750 had not opened Ishara in ninety days, and 16 of those 318 were very disappointed. Among the 432 active, 164 were — 38.0 per cent, identical to wave 2. The gap between 24 and 38 was a difference of eligibility screen, not of finding (Exhibit 6).

Three further things have turned out to be unsafe. Wave 1's 41.0 per cent is not comparable to wave 2's 38.0, because wave 1 was web-only; on web respondents alone wave 2 is 40.0 per cent, a fall of one point rather than three, and neither difference is distinguishable from zero (Exhibit 5). The Tamil response scale used for Coimbatore and Madurai came from a different vendor than the Hindi and Marathi versions, and those cities return the city cut's lowest score, 31.0 per cent — a translation artefact, or the truth. And the WhatsApp flow reversed the option order, a known source of response-order bias; within Udhaar-only users WhatsApp scored 33.3 per cent against web's 22.2, so the channel that reached the real majority returned the friendlier number.

5. The people

Chaitrali Rautray — Vice-President, Product, Pune
Position: report 38.0 per cent, with the weighting shown. Incentive: her option grant vests on the Series B closing. Not saying: she signed off on wave 1's methodology unread, so disowning web-only intercepts disowns her own April note.
Chandresh Radhakrishnan — Co-founder and Chief Executive, Pune
Position: Ishara has fit in Collect; the blend averages a good business with a free one. Incentive: Istaara's bridge at flat valuation avoids a down round. Not saying: on 2 October he told Chaitanya Ratnaparkhi that September was “a little over forty”.
Charuta Ranadive — Co-founder and Chief Technology Officer, Bengaluru
Position: Udhaar-only's 28.9 per cent measures the 2024 deferral, and says what her crash logs have said for two years. Incentive: the rewrite is her unfinished work. Not saying: she doubts it can be done in a quarter either, and her 42-engineer-month estimate for the whole rewrite — of which section 9's 26 months is the first phase — has not been re-based since January.
Chintan Rasal — Head of Field Growth, Indore
Position: the survey is over-read; his 14 field executives talk to shopkeepers daily and none recognises the picture. Incentive: his bonus is on activated accounts, which the free tier supplies. Not saying: he chose the WhatsApp flow's reverse option order himself.
Celine Rouleau — Senior Data Scientist, Toronto
Position: report no single number; give the board the cells and the three weightings and make it choose a base. Incentive: credibility, having been right about the denominator. Not saying: she thinks even the eligible-population weighting is wrong, and her channel-weighted 32.9 per cent stays uncirculated.
Clemens Rauschenberg — Head of Design, Berlin
Position: the instrument is broken before the arithmetic starts; re-write and re-translate wave 3 after cognitive interviews. Incentive: a research budget twice refused. Not saying: he has run eleven such interviews informally, and in nine the shopkeeper did not understand the premise.
Cheryl Raghunathan — Customer Success Lead, Singapore
Position: wave 3 cannot go over WhatsApp before January without a fresh consent notice and a DPDP purpose entry. Incentive: she is named personally in the consent-governance filing. Not saying: she doubts the September fielding was covered as drafted.
Cormac Rafferty — Head of Sales, Gulf and North America, New Jersey
Position: the distributor tier scores 40.0 per cent, carries 40.7 per cent of revenue and holds the only contracts; build for it. Incentive: his commission is on distributor-tier bookings. Not saying: Cherag Rajani has twice asked him about ONDC direct ordering, unreported.

6. Exhibits

7. Voices

“Can we please stop saying ‘the PMF score’ as if there is one. There are 684 people who said very disappointed. Everything after that is a choice about what to divide them by, and five slides make five different choices.”

Celine Rouleau, product-analytics channel, 11 October, 02:14 IST

“Celine, with respect: 46 to 54 per cent for Collect. That is not a rounding argument. The Udhaar number is about a free product we stopped investing in. We know that. We decided that.”

Chandresh Radhakrishnan, reply, 11 October, 08:40 IST

“We decided it. I warned about it. Both are true and only one of them is in the board minute.”

Charuta Ranadive, reply, 11 October, 09:02 IST

“I took the Tamil wording to two shopkeepers in Madurai on Thursday. The first asked me what I meant — if Ishara disappears, where does the twelve thousand rupees Ravi owes him go? He was not answering a question about a product.”

Chintan Rasal, field note circulated 12 October

“Nine out of eleven interviews did not understand the premise. That is not a low score; that is an invalid instrument, and we have built two board slides on it.”

Clemens Rauschenberg, design review, 20 October

“Before anyone plans wave 3: the September fielding went to numbers we hold as account identifiers. I have asked counsel whether the August purpose entry covers research. Do not schedule a January wave until I have the answer.”

Cheryl Raghunathan, email to Chaitrali, 28 October

“The term sheet says the core cohort must be at or above forty. I drafted ‘core cohort’ loosely in July because nobody had a definition. I am not going to supply one for you now.”

Chaitanya Ratnaparkhi, Istaara Ventures, to Chaitrali, 6 November

8. The options as Chaitrali sees them

A. Report 38.0 per cent, and argue the Collect case

Put Exhibit 2 on slide four, say 38.0 per cent, and build the ask around Collect's 50.0 per cent and its 46.1-to-53.9 interval, asking Istaara to read “core cohort” as Collect. Risk: Chandresh has already said “a little over forty” to Chaitanya, so the correction lands as a retraction; and 640 respondents is thin for a ₹24 crore ask.

B. Report nothing until wave 3

Tell the board September is not interpretable and commit to a January re-field with a stratified, app-first intercept and re-translated wording. Risk: Cheryl's consent question is unanswered, so January may not be available; and a board told to wait a quarter will draw its own conclusion.

C. Narrow the company

Take the eligible-weighted 33.5 per cent at face value as the verdict on Udhaar-only, stop investing in it, and concentrate on Collect and the distributor tier — 67.8 per cent of revenue and 25.0 per cent of eligible accounts. Risk: Udhaar-only is the funnel, Chintan's activation bonus and the field motion run on it, and 28.9 per cent may measure neglect rather than demand.

D. Fund the ledger rewrite and take the penalty

Treat Charuta's reading as correct, start the rewrite now, miss the 31 January date and accept the ₹18 lakh service credit to Izdihaar. Risk: ₹18 lakh is 55.6 per cent of that account's annual value, and the relationship rather than the credit is at stake; and the rewrite rests on crash logs and a score Celine calls the least reliable number on the page.

Chaitrali had written all four on a sheet of paper and then, some time after eleven, a fifth line under them, circled: all four assume the survey is a verdict. Every option treats the number as a measurement of the product, not of the instrument, the sample, or what a shopkeeper in Madurai thinks he is being asked when a stranger invites him to imagine that his customers' debts have vanished. Option C does worse: as she had written it, it reads the company-wide blend of 33.5 per cent as though it were the Udhaar-only score of 28.9 — the dashboard's slip in the opposite direction. And Clemens's nine interviews were not in the pack, nor was the fact that Ishara had never asked, in any coded form, the second and third questions Sean Ellis's method calls for: who the very-disappointed users are, and what they would use instead.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

Cash at 30 September 2026 was ₹18.60 crore. Monthly gross operating cost is ₹1.87 crore against ₹44.98 lakh of revenue, a net burn of ₹1.42 crore. October's burn leaves ₹17.18 crore at 31 October, the balance the board paper must carry, because the paper is dated November. At an unchanged burn that is 12.1 months from 31 October, to about the first week of November 2027. The three overseas roles cost ₹3.36 crore a year, ₹28.00 lakh a month, about 15 per cent of monthly cost; a Pune Android engineer is fully loaded at ₹38 lakh a year.

Istaara's bridge is ₹24 crore at the Series A valuation, conditional on a September product–market fit score at or above 40 per cent for “the core cohort”, a term the term sheet does not define and Chaitanya Ratnaparkhi will not. Engineering has nine engineers uncommitted from 10 November to 31 January — 82 days, about 2.7 months, so roughly 24.3 engineer-months at full utilisation. The Arabic and VAT work is estimated at 11 engineer-months and the first phase of the ledger rewrite at 26; together they are 37, half again what exists, and on these dates the rewrite phase does not fit even on its own. Cheryl's consent question means no WhatsApp fielding can be scheduled before counsel replies. The board pack is due to six people by 21:00 IST on Monday, 9 November, and the board meets on Thursday, 12 November.

At twenty past midnight Chaitrali opened the slide again. The title field still read Product–market fit: September update; below it the chart placeholder sat empty. She typed 38.0%, looked at it, deleted it, typed 684 people, looked at that a long while, then got up to put the karanji away before the ants found it. Outside, one last string of crackers went off over the lane; in Toronto it was two in the afternoon, and Celine was rebuilding the channel weights again.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. State what population each of the seven denominators in Exhibit 1 describes. Which, if any, is the right base for the question Ishara is trying to answer, and why?
  2. Exhibit 2 shows completion falling monotonically from the top box to the bottom. Explain the mechanism producing the dashboard's 44.0 per cent, and say whether it also threatens the 38.0 per cent figure.
  3. Exhibit 6(a) reports 24.0 per cent and Exhibit 3 reports 38.0. Are these two findings or one? What would you need to decide, and what does your answer imply about publishing a single PMF score at all?
  4. Exhibit 4(b) offers 38.0, 33.5 and 39.1 per cent, all correctly computed, and none of them the Udhaar-only score. Which does the board need, which does Chaitrali, which does Charuta? If they differ, what does that say about the Sean Ellis question as a company-level metric?
  5. Exhibit 5(a) shows neither wave could have detected a three-point move. Within the constraints in section 9, design the smallest change to instrument and sample that would let Ishara distinguish a wording problem from a product problem — and say what you would still be unable to learn.
  6. It is Monday morning, 9 November. What figure, if any, goes on slide four, and what does Chaitrali say to the board on Thursday — about the number, the July 2024 decision, and the bridge condition nobody will define?

Discovery & Design · Quantitative & Market Research

Would They Be Very Disappointed? The Sean Ellis PMF Survey

One question, three boxes, and a 40 percent line that a lot of product teams treat as a verdict when it was only ever meant to be a pointer.

1. A board deck due in nine days

On the second Monday of February 2026, Ananya Krishnan, VP of Product at Anveshan Health, a Bengaluru teleconsultation app with 640,000 monthly active users, opened a spreadsheet she had been avoiding for a week. Anveshan's Series B pitch was set for the following Wednesday, and the lead investor's associate had asked, almost as an aside on a diligence call, "How do you know you actually have product-market fit, versus a lot of people trying you once during a WhatsApp forward about your ₹49 doctor consultations?" Ananya did not have a crisp answer. Daily active users had grown 18 percent quarter over quarter, but thirty-day retention had drifted from 34 percent to 29 percent over the same stretch, and nobody on the founding team could say with confidence whether the company was building something people needed or something people were merely trying.

The number at stake was concrete: Anveshan was raising ₹42 crore at a valuation that assumed durable demand, not a festival-season spike. If Ananya walked into the board meeting with only vanity growth charts, the round would likely get repriced downward, or stall while the fund's partners debated whether Anveshan was a feature or a company. She needed a signal that was cheap to gather, hard to fake, and legible to people outside product. Her co-founder, Rohit Bhandari, suggested the tool a growth advisor had mentioned in passing eight months earlier and the team had never gotten around to running: the Sean Ellis PMF survey.

2. The idea, stated plainly

The Sean Ellis PMF survey is a single question, asked of people who have actually used a product, with three possible answers: "How would you feel if you could no longer use [product]?" — Very disappointed, Somewhat disappointed, Not disappointed (because I don't really use it). The score that matters is the share of respondents who pick "Very disappointed." Ellis, a growth marketer who worked with Dropbox, LogMeIn and several early-2000s software companies before coining the term "growth hacking," built the survey because he needed a way to decide, quickly and cheaply, whether a product was worth pouring marketing spend into before it had earned genuine pull. Spend acquires users regardless of whether the product is any good; Ellis wanted a filter that told him whether the product deserved that spend at all.

The idea rests on a simple behavioral premise: people who would genuinely miss a product if it vanished are telling you it occupies a real place in their life or work — a job previously done badly, expensively, or not at all. People who would shrug are telling you the product rides on convenience or a promotion, not on unmet need. Having studied survey results across roughly a hundred startups he advised, Ellis proposed a rule of thumb: products that cross 40 percent "very disappointed" tend to have an easier time growing, because word of mouth and reduced churn start doing work paid acquisition would otherwise have to do alone. The sentence Ananya could say in the boardroom without sounding glib was this: "We asked our actual users how they'd feel losing us, and told you exactly what the answer distribution was — not what we hoped it would be."

3. How it actually works, step by step

The mechanics look deceptively simple, which is why teams get the setup wrong. The first and most consequential decision is whom to survey. Ellis's method targets people who have used the product enough to have an opinion — not every signup, and not lapsed users who forgot it existed. For Anveshan, that meant Ananya had to define an "active user" threshold before writing a single question: anyone who had completed at least two teleconsultations in the preceding thirty days, excluding one-time trial users and dormant accounts still registered but functionally gone.

Second, the question is asked exactly as worded, without softening it into something like "How satisfied are you?" — a different question that measures a different thing. Satisfaction is about whether the last experience met expectations; disappointment-at-loss measures attachment, which is closer to what predicts retention and referral. Third, practitioners add follow-up questions that are easy to skip but carry most of the diagnostic value: the primary benefit gained, who would most benefit from the product, and — the one teams forget most often — what the user would use instead if it disappeared. That last answer tells you who your real competitive set is, often not who you assumed.

Fourth comes distribution and timing: the survey typically goes out by email or in-app prompt, to a random sample of the active cohort rather than whoever is easiest to reach, sent when the user has recently engaged so the experience is fresh but not so immediate that it captures a single transaction's mood rather than a settled relationship with the product. Finally, and this is the step most teams skip, results need to be cut by segment before anyone reports a single top-line number — a blended average across very different user types usually hides the one segment where fit is real.

4. The arithmetic, run twice

Ananya's team invited 850 users who met the two-consultation threshold. Of those, 312 completed the survey — a 36.7 percent response rate, worth noting since rates well under 30 percent tend to skew toward people with strong opinions in either direction. The raw distribution came back as follows.

ResponseCountShare of 312
Very disappointed11837.8%
Somewhat disappointed14044.9%
Not disappointed5417.3%
Total respondents312100%

The headline PMF score is 118 ÷ 312 = 0.378, or 37.8 percent — just under Ellis's 40 percent marker. Read at face value, that is a mildly disappointing number for a board deck: close, but short, easy for a skeptical investor to wave away as "almost there." Ananya's first instinct, and the mistake many product leads make at exactly this point, was to treat 37.8 percent as the final word.

Rohit pushed for a second pass before anyone presented anything: cut the same 312 responses by why the person used the app. Two cohorts emerged — first-time users who had tried Anveshan for a single acute complaint (a fever, a skin rash) and were unlikely to return soon regardless of experience quality, and repeat users managing an ongoing condition such as diabetes or hypertension, using the app monthly for prescription renewal. Re-running the arithmetic on only the chronic-care segment — 90 of the 312 respondents — produced a different picture.

Chronic-care segmentCountShare of 90
Very disappointed4145.6%
Somewhat disappointed3741.1%
Not disappointed1213.3%
Total in segment90100%

In this narrower cut, 41 ÷ 90 = 0.456, or 45.6 percent — comfortably past the 40 percent line. The acute, one-off users were diluting the blended score not because Anveshan had failed them, but because a single-episode teleconsultation is a weaker habit than a recurring one, and disappointment-at-loss is fundamentally a question about habits. The second pass did not change any user's answer; it changed which users Ananya averaged together, and that choice moved the conclusion from "not quite there" to "clearly there, in one segment."

5. Nuances a learner must sit with

Sampling only active users flatters the score by design

Because the survey excludes people who never engaged enough to qualify, the percentage describes attachment among those who stuck around, not conversion across the full funnel. A product can post an impressive 50 percent PMF score among active users while ninety percent of signups have already quietly left, and the survey alone will not surface that gap.

The 40 percent threshold is a heuristic, not a law

Ellis derived it from a specific, mostly software sample studied roughly fifteen years ago. Categories differ: utilities that solve an acute pain point (accounting software, password managers) often clear 40 percent more easily than discretionary entertainment products, where even beloved apps sit lower because "disappointed" is a strong word for something optional. Treat the number as a comparison point within your own category and trend line, not a universal pass mark.

Response rate shapes the answer

Low response rates, as with Anveshan's 36.7 percent, tend to overrepresent people with strong feelings in either direction, since indifferent users skip surveys. A score built on a 12 percent response rate deserves far less confidence than the identical percentage built on a 55 percent response rate, even though both get reported as one clean number.

It is a correlate of good outcomes, not a cause of them

Crossing 40 percent does not make a company grow; it is an indicator that has historically accompanied companies that did. Confusing signal for mechanism leads teams to chase the survey number itself — nudging wording, timing sends after a support success — rather than doing the product work the number was meant to reflect.

It is routinely confused with satisfaction and with NPS

Net Promoter Score asks whether a user would recommend the product, blending quality with social risk and category norms. Satisfaction measures the most recent experience. The PMF survey asks about loss, tapping something closer to habit and switching cost. A product can have high satisfaction and a mediocre PMF score if users like it but would barely notice its disappearance.

It cannot tell you what to build next

The number identifies whether attachment exists somewhere in the base; it says nothing about which feature to prioritize or how to price. That work still requires interviews, usage data and judgment — the survey narrows where to look, most usefully through its "what would you use instead" follow-up, but it does not do the looking for you.

Timing distorts the result in both directions

Survey too early, before a habit forms, and the score reads artificially low. Survey only lapsed users and it reads low for a different reason — the disappointed ones already left. Survey right after a support success or a discount and it reads artificially high. The honest window is a representative slice of genuinely active users, asked in the ordinary course of use.

The question a thoughtful newcomer should ask first

Before trusting any reported PMF percentage, ask: who exactly was invited, what fraction responded, and was the number reported blended or broken out by segment? A clean percentage with no answer to those three questions is not evidence of fit — it is a number waiting to be interrogated.

6. Consumer, B2B, marketplace — and startup versus scale-up

In a pure consumer product like Anveshan, the survey is relatively clean: one type of user, one relationship to the product, and the main risk is forgetting to exclude the merely curious from the merely committed. B2B software complicates the picture because the person who evaluates or buys the product — an IT administrator, a finance lead — often has a different relationship to it than the daily end user typing into it. A vendor selling expense-management software might find finance-admin buyers giving very different disappointment answers than employees who file receipts through it once a month, and reporting only the buyer's view can quietly overstate fit among people who actually live inside the product every day.

Marketplaces add a second-sided version of the same problem. A ride-hailing marketplace such as Poochtaach Mobility must survey riders and drivers separately, since a driver's disappointment-at-loss depends on income substitution — could they earn the same elsewhere — while a rider's depends on convenience and price relative to alternatives. A blended score across both sides usually means very little, since it averages two structurally different relationships to the same product. Early-stage companies work with small, noisy samples where a single enthusiastic cohort of fifty early adopters can produce a flattering number that won't survive a broader audience; the discipline is to treat any score as provisional and re-run it as the base grows. Large, established companies use the survey differently — not as a one-time verdict but as a tracked metric alongside retention curves, re-run quarterly or after major launches, watching the trend and the segment mix rather than one snapshot.

7. Common mistakes

Mistake one: surveying the whole user base, active and inactive alike. The symptom is a PMF score that swings wildly between rounds for no apparent reason. The error is skipping the activity threshold that makes the question answerable — someone who used the product once has no informed opinion about losing it. The cheapest diagnostic: check, before sending, whether an explicit "active user" definition was written down and applied to the invite list.

Mistake two: treating 40 percent as a funding gate. The symptom is a team quietly tweaking wording, timing, or the invite list until the topline number crosses the line. The error is mistaking a directional heuristic, built from one dataset in one era, for a pass-fail test. The cheapest diagnostic: ask whether anyone has read the "what would you use instead" answers recently, or whether the number is the only thing discussed.

Mistake three: running the survey once and filing it away. The symptom is a company still citing a PMF score from eighteen months earlier in a board deck. The error is treating the survey as a one-time certification rather than a recurring instrument, like a retention chart. The cheapest diagnostic: check the date on the last survey — if nobody can answer quickly, it has been too long.

Mistake four: reporting only the blended top-line number. The symptom is a score stuck in the high 20s or low 30s quarter after quarter despite visible product improvements. The error is averaging structurally different segments into one figure and never cutting it apart. The cheapest diagnostic: re-run the arithmetic on the two or three most obvious segments — new versus repeat, one use case versus another — before concluding anything.

8. What good looks like

Consider a fintech contemporary of Anveshan's, a savings-and-investing app, whose product lead ran the identical survey the same quarter. She defined active users as those with at least one transaction in sixty days, achieved a 51 percent response rate by sending through the app's own push channel rather than email, and reported three numbers to her board instead of one: the blended score, the score among users with an automated monthly investment (higher, since automation signals habit), and the score among users who had only ever made a single manual deposit (lower, for the same reason). She paired the survey with five follow-up calls to "somewhat disappointed" respondents, asking what would move them to "very." The board left with a segmented, falsifiable story about where fit existed — exactly the clarity Ananya had to build through a second pass rather than a first instinct.

9. What Ananya decided

Ananya did not present 37.8 percent, nor did she overstate matters by presenting only 45.6 percent as if it described the whole company. She presented both, explicitly labeled, alongside retention data showing chronic-care users retained at more than double the rate of acute, single-episode users. Her recommendation to the board was to reallocate marketing budget from broad acute-care acquisition toward chronic-care patient acquisition and toward converting existing acute-care users into recurring relationships — a strategy grounded in where the survey said real attachment already lived, not one aimed at nudging the blended percentage upward through wording or sampling tricks. The investor's associate, seeing the segmented breakdown and the interview notes behind it, told Ananya afterward that the honesty of the cut was more persuasive than a clean 40-plus number would have been alone.

What Ananya's team should study next, once the survey has done its narrow job, is retention cohort analysis and qualitative churn interviews — tools that explain why the acute-care segment falls away rather than merely confirming that it does. Two questions are worth sitting with: first, if you changed your definition of "active user" by a few days, would your score move enough to change the decision you're about to make with it? Second, are you running this survey to learn something you don't yet know, or to produce a number you can defend in a meeting whose outcome you've already decided?

case20v1-q.pmf.survey:
Haveli Pantry and the Disappointment Question

A decision case on the Sean Ellis product-market-fit survey

1. Opening

On the morning of Wednesday, 14 October 2026, Bhairavi Pilankar, Head of Product at Haveli Pantry, sat in the company's Pune office with a spreadsheet she had been refreshing since seven. Diwali fell on 8 November. Her chief executive, Balaji Pillai, had asked her to tell him by Wednesday, 21 October whether Haveli should commit to its largest ever festive campaign, a nationwide gift-box push that required purchase orders to the company's ghee and oil suppliers within the week.

The evidence she had been asked to weigh was a single survey question, put to customers a month earlier: How would you feel if you could no longer use Haveli Pantry? The answer was in the spreadsheet. It did not say what Balaji wanted it to say, and it did not say the opposite either.

2. Company background

Haveli Pantry sells small-batch, traceable staples to urban households: A2 bilona ghee, cold-pressed groundnut and sesame oils, stone-ground flours and millets. Founded in 2022 by Balaji Pillai and two classmates, it ships from a Pune fulfilment centre and takes orders through its own app. Customers may buy once, or subscribe to a monthly or fortnightly basket delivered with a fixed price lock.

The competitive map is crowded. Amul and Tata Consumer's Sampann own the shelf in the mass market; BigBasket and the premium grocers own the considered purchase; and the quick-commerce players, Zepto, Swiggy Instamart and Blinkit, have made ten-minute delivery of everyday staples feel normal. Haveli's argument is provenance rather than speed: a customer can scan a QR code on the jar and see the farm, the batch and the lab report. Payments run on UPI and the company is registered under GST like any food seller; its labelling is subject to FSSAI rules, which its compliance consultant reviews each quarter.

As of 15 September 2026 Haveli had 41,500 registered users. Annual revenue was ₹38 crore, of which subscriptions contributed roughly half. The company had raised ₹14 crore in two rounds and had about fourteen months of runway, which is why a ₹1.8 crore festive bet mattered: with ₹7 crore of cash and a monthly burn of ₹50 lakh, the company had 14 months of runway.

3. The situation

Gifting is where Balaji sees the next stage of the company. A Dubai-based hospitality group had indicated interest in 1,500 Diwali boxes for its staff and guests, and Haveli's two regional sales leads were pitching similar orders to Bengaluru and Mumbai employers. The festive plan assumed that customers loved the product enough to give it as a present under their own name, which is a stronger claim than that they enjoyed buying it.

In September Bhairavi had run the one-question survey that Sean Ellis popularised while advising early software companies. His observation was that products people are headed for success with tend to have a large share of users who say they would be very disappointed without them, and that around 40 per cent was a useful dividing line. It is a benchmark drawn from his experience of many startups, not a law, and it measures a feeling, not future purchases.

Bhairavi restricted the survey to users who had actually experienced the product: those with at least two delivered orders in the 90 days ending 15 September. That produced 9,600 eligible users. All 9,600 were invited by WhatsApp and email between 16 and 30 September. By the 30 September close, 1,200 had answered the disappointment question. Eligibility was fixed by orders up to 15 September, so some respondents who qualified then had stopped ordering or cancelled by the time they answered; 60 of them chose "I no longer use it". 4. The people

Balaji Pillai, co-founder and chief executive, is in Mumbai, meeting investors. He reads the subscriber figure of 52.5 per cent as proof that the gifting bet is safe, since subscribers are the people most likely to gift. He wants a yes or no by 21 October and a campaign live by 26 October.

Bhrigu Pednekar, the company's data scientist in Toronto, built the extract. Working in a time zone nine and a half hours behind Pune, he sends his notes overnight. His worry is the response gap in Exhibit 3: subscribers answered at 16.0 per cent and others at 10.9 per cent. If the invited population were reweighted to its true mix, 3,000 subscribers at 52.5 per cent and 6,600 others at 23.3 per cent would give 1,575 plus 1,540, or 3,115 very-disappointed users out of 9,600, a population-weighted score of 32.4 per cent. He cautions that this assumes non-responders resemble responders in their own segment, which nobody knows.

Bina Paliwal leads customer success from Singapore, where she also serves a small group of overseas Indian customers who order for parents in India. Her tickets show subscribers asking for gift wrapping unprompted, but also one-time buyers complaining about late delivery during the festive rush in Chennai and Hyderabad. She would hate to see the company promise a gift experience it cannot reliably deliver.

Bhairavi Pilankar, the protagonist, owns the product roadmap and has to recommend an option. She is not against gifting. She is against reading a 52.5 per cent score from the 16.0 per cent of eligible subscribers who answered as a finding about everybody.

5. The options

Option A: Commit the full ₹180 lakh. Of this, ₹110 lakh buys inventory and gift packaging and ₹70 lakh buys paid media. Management's estimate is ₹3.0 crore of festive sales if the subscriber signal generalises. Place the supplier orders, buy the paid media, and accept the Dubai group's 1,500-box request. The upside is the largest festive revenue Haveli has had and the possibility that gifting becomes a second engine. The cost is concentration: if the 35.0 per cent overall score, or the weighted 32.4 per cent, is nearer to the truth than 52.5 per cent, much of the inventory is aimed at customers who would shrug.

Option B: Stand down the campaign and spend ₹95 lakh on the core product. This is ₹45 lakh for packaging and delivery-time guarantees, ₹30 lakh for reorder reminders and app work, and ₹20 lakh for courier incentives; no festive revenue uplift is expected. Redirect the money to delivery reliability, packaging and a reorder reminder for non-subscribers, aiming to lift the 23.3 per cent segment. The upside is that it attacks the weakest group directly. The cost is missing Diwali, the single largest buying moment of the year, and a Dubai client that will turn to someone else.

Option C: Run a narrow, staged festive push of ₹55 lakh and a ₹4 lakh follow-up. Of the ₹55 lakh, ₹30 lakh buys gift boxes and ₹25 lakh buys media on subscriber-look-alike audiences, with boxes for existing subscribers only, sized to 40 per cent of the Dubai request, which is 600 of the 1,500 boxes. Spend ₹4 lakh on incentives for a second-wave survey to a random sample of the 8,400 invited users who did not answer. Management's estimate is ₹1.2 crore of festive sales. The upside is a test of whether the 52.5 per cent holds beyond the people who volunteer. The cost is lower upside if the subscriber signal is real, and a partial answer to the Dubai client.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. Who was eligible, how many were asked, and how many answered? On which base is the 35.0 per cent computed, and does the 12.5 per cent response rate make it more or less trustworthy?
  2. Why does the subscriber score of 52.5 per cent not simply replace the headline? What would have to be true about the 2,520 subscribers who did not answer for it to hold?
  3. Bhrigu's weighted 32.4 per cent and the variant 36.8 per cent (lapsed users removed) both differ from 35.0 per cent. Which would you report to the board, and why?
  4. Which of the three options best fits the evidence by 21 October, and what would make you change your mind before 8 November?

7. A note for the learner

The Ellis survey is a leading indicator of fit, not a forecast of sales. It tells you how much a product would be missed by people who know it, and it is only as good as the base it is calculated on. Three disciplines frame this case. First, state the base: 420 of 1,200 respondents, from 9,600 eligible, from 41,500 registered. Second, notice that a segment, not the overall figure, is where a score tends to be informative; a clear signal in one group is a hypothesis about a market, not evidence of one. Third, treat the 40 per cent figure as a benchmark that invites inquiry, not a pass mark: the 95 per cent interval for the overall score is 32.3 to 37.7 per cent, and for the subscribers it is 48.0 to 57.0 per cent.

A defensible path is Option C. It does not pretend that 35.0 per cent proves failure, nor that 52.5 per cent proves fit across the board. It puts money behind the group where the signal is strongest, keeps the 21 October deadline, and buys the one thing the survey lacks: evidence from the quiet 8,400. Its weakness is that it concedes part of the Dubai order, and a student who prefers Option A should be asked what would happen if the non-responders look like the non-subscribers. A student who prefers Option B should be asked what a better delivery experience costs in lost festive weeks. The point of the lens is not to produce one right answer, but to make the evidence behind each choice explicit.
